prize_parts.citation: For visionary, densely patterned prose that builds memory, the body and dream into an expansive metaphysical imaginative project.

statement.case_for: My first-round preference for Cărtărescu rests on the criterion of a voice that is found in this writer's work and nowhere else. Working from public knowledge and the supplied description, the Orbitor (Blinding) trilogy and Solenoid appear to be works of unusual formal ambition and imaginative depth. In them, dense and patterned sentences carry a private cosmology of memory, the body and dream. The poetry and earlier prose appear to be the formative ground of the large novels, and the late work seems to extend the project in scale rather than repeat it. This is a case about sustained quality and distinctiveness of voice. It does not depend on reputation, nationality or political symbolism. I have reconsidered the alternatives on literary grounds. Carson, Michon, Zurita and Murnane each have a recognisable voice and real formal achievement. On what I can assess, none combines that distinctiveness with the same scale of sustained imaginative architecture across a multi-decade oeuvre. A single-laureate citation would be clear and would cover the prose and poetry of one Romanian-language writer.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the effect of this prose depends on Romanian syntax, rhythm and register, and I am judging it through translation and general public knowledge. I have not independently verified the texts. Some of the very long, digressive novels may show overextension rather than purposeful pattern. If so, the claim of sustained quality across the whole body of work would be weaker than the best volumes suggest. Coverage of the poetry and early stories is also thinner than coverage of the large novels, so the citation scope is better supported for the late prose than for the whole oeuvre.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Carson first. He argues that her hybrid forms remake the boundaries of classical scholarship, lyric, translation, essay and book design. He treats her engagement with Greek and Latin sources as living material rather than ornament. He also notes that the case rests heavily on a few hybrid works, that some output is slight or occasional, and that her relation to the 'idealistic tendency' of Nobel's will is open to debate.
responses.response: I agree that Carson's voice is unmistakable and that the classical engagement is substantive. That is why I keep her as an alternative and not lower. His own reservations are the ones that decide it for me. If the strongest effects of Autobiography of Red and Nox depend on book-object form and on classical reference, the evidence for sustained quality across a whole oeuvre is narrower than it first appears. How much weight her translations carry as original authorship also complicates a single citation. Cărtărescu's achievement sits more fully in the written sentence and in a coherent imaginative architecture across several large works. I would still take seriously the point that his project may be as translation-dependent as hers. I do not think the 'idealistic tendency' question separates the two candidates clearly, because both can be argued under it.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu first. She credits a visionary prose voice and a large, coherent imaginative project. She also warns that translation may not carry the stylistic density, that the poetry and early fiction are less well known, and that some very long, digressive books may divide readers on sustained quality.
responses.response: Her last point is the one I take most seriously, and I share it. The question is whether the density is purposeful pattern or at times overextension. It cannot be settled from an overview; it requires reading the whole corpus. I would not take it as a reason to look elsewhere, since every other candidate faces a comparable limit of translation or compactness. But I would not treat 'established internationally' as evidence of sustained quality. Her caution that the citation should not be narrowed to an 'Eastern European postmodern' label seems right to me. The wording should rest on the metaphysical and corporeal imagination and on the language.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg puts Cărtărescu first and Murnane second. He sees in Murnane a radically inward fiction with an austere, self-questioning syntax and a very consistent voice. He also notes that its significance beyond a committed readership is uncertain because the scope is deliberately narrow.
responses.response: I rank Murnane fifth. I respect the voice and the formal discipline, which I would also call a voice found nowhere else. My difference is about breadth and growth. A deliberately closed method can deepen its concerns, but across an oeuvre it is harder to show development than in a work that expands in scale. I take his point that narrowness is a feature of the method and not a flaw. Still, I would want the committee to ask whether the repeated procedures yield enough variety over the whole corpus. I also do not think Cărtărescu's scale is automatically a virtue. Sem-Sandberg's own caution about uneven quality across very long books applies to him as much as to Murnane's narrowness.

responses.point: Palm places Wright third. She stresses the formal renewal of the novel through oral forms, sovereignty and ecological time. She also notes that the oeuvre is smaller than that of many rivals, and that the work should not be read mainly through political symbolism.
responses.response: I ranked Wright sixth, but I agree with Palm's framing. The merit has to be judged on the narrative form and the invented idiom, and the political and collective-memory content is realised through that form. The formal scale of Carpentaria and The Swan Book is a real achievement. My hesitation is the same one Palm names: a small number of very large books makes it harder to judge sustained quality and growth. I also acknowledge that I may not read Aboriginal English and the oral-tradition elements fully. That is a limit of my own reading and should not be counted against the work. For me this is a question of timing and breadth of corpus, not a question of quality.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's voice survives translation. Romanian syntax, rhythm and register cannot be assessed directly from the English and French versions.
Whether the density and length of the later novels is sustained, purposeful pattern or at times overextension. Only a close reading of the whole corpus could settle this.
Coverage of the poetry and early stories in translation is thin, so the citation scope is better supported for the late prose than for the whole oeuvre.

For the alternatives, how to weigh Carson's translations and book-object works as literary achievement, and how far Michon's small corpus and French-dependent style limit assessment of significance across the body of work.
I rely on public knowledge and the supplied descriptions, and I have not independently verified any text.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile.
